attributes.title: Level 1

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you brainstorm the functions that might be added to code the golf ball’s movement in the first Build activity?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How does the structure of Red Belt Build activities differ from previous belts in IMPACT?

❓ What functions might be used to code the golf ball’s movement in the first Build activity?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja how the structure of Red Belt will differ from prior belts in IMPACT. In Red Belt, multiple Build activities across the level will be used to construct a larger, complex project based on a given theme (instead of multiple, individual projects). The starter code for each successive Build activity will be populated with code from the previous Build activity. At the end of the level, the ninja will have an opportunity to create their own complex project to add to their Red Belt portfolio, using theme-specific concepts applied throughout the Build activities.

💡 Prompt the ninja to brainstorm specific functions that might be needed to code the golf ball’s movement in this first Build activity. Encourage the ninja to write down ideas as pseudocode to think through the sequence and the logic of the mini golf code.
steps.instructions:
Welcome to Red Belt Level 1!


This is the first of 3 Build activities where you will create a mini golf project! Each Build activity will build off the previous activity’s code to create one complete project by the end of the level. 


In the first Build activity, you will code the foundation of the mini golf level. You’ll use physics, friction, absolute value, and the status bar extension to code the golf ball’s movement, in order to make it feel like a real game of mini golf!


How might the user impact sprite movement on screen?

steps.hints: ❓ Did you notice where walls are strategically placed in the levelOne tilemap asset?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What do you notice about the levelOne tilemap asset?

❓ What might each tile type be used for in the mini golf project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to notice the different tiles in My Assets and how they are incorporated into the levelOne tilemap asset. 

💡 Ask the ninja why walls are added in certain places (such as the top of the windmill tile), but not in others (such as the hole tile). Prompt the ninja to consider how tilemap walls will affect the sprite’s movement and trigger overlap events.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by exploring the code already in the editor and the assets in My Assets.


Click the Assets menu along the top of the screen and notice the variety of top down and 2D mini golf themed tile assets, as well as both top down and 2D tilemaps. These assets will be used across 3 Build activities to create a complete mini golf project.


Open the levelOne tilemap asset. Notice that it is longer than the width of the screen and how the 2D tiles in My Tiles are used to design the first hole of the course.

steps.hints: ❓ Does the background image appear in a natural position behind the golf course?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What images are used for the Player and Ball sprites? 

❓ What might each sprite be used for in the mini golf project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the nina to notice the existing code in the JavaScript editor and consider how each sprite and sprite kind will be used in the project.

💡 Make sure the ninja has set the background image and tilemap before the two sprites so that they appear in the correct sequence on screen.
steps.instructions:
Display the tilemap on screen!


Return to the JavaScript editor, then add code to display the backgroundImage asset and levelOne tilemap on screen above the code that creates the Player and Ball sprites. 


Click ▶ to test the background image and tilemap code.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use the setPosition function to add or subtract pixels from the Ball sprite’s x and y-positions to set the Player sprite’s position?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What values might be used to set the Ball and Player sprite’s positions?

❓ What does the sprite’s x-friction represent?

❓ What symbols should be used to set the Ball sprite’s x-friction (fx)?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja that the x-friction (fx) value represents the force opposing a sprite’s motion in the horizontal direction. This will cause the sprite’s speed to decrease because it needs to overcome the force opposing it. Prompt the ninja why it might be useful to add friction to a sprite’s movement, and how this mimics how objects move in real life.
steps.instructions:
Position the Ball and Player sprites on the tilemap!﻿


Use the setPosition function to place the Ball sprite on the tilemap, so that it appears slightly to the right of the tee off tile. Then, use the Ball sprite’s x and y-positions to set the Player sprite’s position. Add or subtract pixels to display the Player sprite slightly to the left of the Ball sprite and so that the bottom of the club image aligns with the Ball sprite.


Then, set the Ball sprite’s y-acceleration so that it will be pulled down to the ground, once hit. Set its x-friction (fx) value to 50. This value represents the horizontal opposing force against the motion of a sprite, causing its movement to slow after it’s been hit. Set the camera to follow the Ball sprite, too.


Click ▶ to test the Ball and Player sprites’ position code.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the Ball sprite’s vy to force multiplied by -1?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What does the force variable control?

❓ What happens when the A button is released?

❓ Why is the Ball sprite’s y-velocity set to the negative equivalent of force?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The force variable sets the x and y-velocity of the Ball sprite. Later in the project, a status bar will be added to allow the user to control the amount of power that the ball is hit with.

💡 When the A button is released, the Player sprite’s position is set to the Ball sprite’s position, simulating the club hitting the ball. After 100 ms, the Player sprite disappears from the screen and the Ball sprite’s velocity is set, causing it to move through the air on screen.

💡 The Ball sprite’s y-velocity set to the negative equivalent of force so that it moves up on the screen, simulating how it would be hit into the air by the golf club.
steps.instructions:
Hit the ball when the A button is released!


Under // project initialization, declare a force variable set to 100.


Add a // project events comment with an A button released event underneath. Assign the Player sprite’s x-position equal to the Ball sprite’s x-position inside the event, so that the club appears to move towards the ball.


Add the Timers extension to the project. Inside the event, use the after function to update each sprite’s properties after 100 ms. Inside the function, set the Player sprite’s Invisible sprite flag on, set the Ball sprite’s x-velocity to the value of the force variable, and its y-velocity to the negative equivalent of force, so that the Ball sprite moves up on the screen. 


Now, the user will be able to see the club make contact with the ball before the ball moves across the tilemap.


Click ▶ to test what happens when the A button is released.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you copy the setPosition code that sets the Player sprite’s position relative to the Ball sprite’s coordinates, and paste it inside the A button pressed event?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the A button is pressed?

❓ Where does the Player sprite appear after the ball is hit?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja to copy the setPosition code that sets the Player sprite’s position and paste it into the A button pressed event, so that it always appears to the left of the Ball sprite.

💡 Prompt the ninja to consider why resetting the Player sprite’s position each time the A button is pressed improves the user experience of the project. By having the golf club image reappear each time the golf ball is ready to be hit, it creates a more realistic representation of the golfing experience.
steps.instructions:
Reset the Player and Ball sprites when the A button is pressed again!


Under // project events, add an A button pressed event. 


Inside the event, reset the Player sprite’s position so that it appears to the left of the Ball sprite, and turn the Player sprite’s Invisible sprite flag off. Because the Player sprite’s position is set relative to the Ball sprite’s coordinates, the club will always appear to the left of the ball, regardless of its position on the tilemap.


Click ▶ to test what happens when the A button is pressed and released.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use conditionals to check if the Ball sprite’s x-velocity is equal to 0 inside the A button pressed event and if ballMoving is false inside the A button released event?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where should the status of the ballMoving variable be updated?

❓ What value would the Ball sprite’s x-velocity be equal to if it is not moving?

❓ What symbol should be used to check that the Ball sprite is not moving when the A button is released?

 

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The ballMoving variable should be set at the beginning of the project, then updated whenever the A button is pressed or released. This will allow the user to keep track of the Ball sprite’s velocity to determine when it can and cannot be hit again.

💡 Prompt the ninja to use a conditional inside the A button pressed event to check the value of the Ball sprite’s x-velocity.
steps.instructions:
Oh no! The user can continue to hit the ball, even while it’s in mid-air! 


Use a variable to keep track of whether the Ball sprite is moving or not. Declare a ballMoving variable and set it to false at the beginning of the project.


Inside the A button pressed event, use the Ball sprite’s x-velocity to check if it is not moving, then update the value of the ballMoving variable accordingly. Cut and paste the code that sets the Player sprite’s position and sprite flag inside the conditional.


Inside the A button released event, check if the ballMoving variable is  false after 100 ms. Then, update the value of the variable once the Ball sprite is moving. Cut and paste the code that sets the Player’s sprite flag and Ball sprite velocity inside the conditional.


Now, the project will check the status of the Ball sprite before allowing the user to hit the ball again.


Click ▶ to test the Ball sprite’s updated movement.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the Ball sprite to bounce on walls when the A button is pressed?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ When should the Ball sprite be set to bounce on walls?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The Ball sprite should be set to bounce on walls whenever the A button is pressed. This will prevent the ball from getting stuck on the tilemap whenever it hits an obstacle.
steps.instructions:
Use a sprite flag to prevent the Ball sprite from getting stuck when it hits a wall obstacle on the tilemap!


Set the Ball sprite to bounce on walls whenever the A button is pressed, so that it has more momentum when it hits an obstacle.


Click ▶ test what happens when the Ball sprite hits an obstacle.

steps.hints:
❓ Did you use the abs function to check if the absolute value of the Ball sprite’s y-velocity is greater than 50 in either direction, like this?

Math.abs(sprite.vy) > 50
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why is the absolute value of the Ball sprite’s y-velocity needed to gradually decrease its speed?

❓ What sprite kind should be used in the onHitWall event?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja to change the sprite kind to Ball in the onHitWall event.

💡 Explain the purpose of the absolute value to the ninja. Remind the ninja that negative or positive values indicate the direction that a sprite is moving in; when the Ball sprite is bouncing up, its y-velocity is a negative value and when it is bouncing down, its y-velocity is a positive value. However, the size of the number indicates the speed that the sprite is moving in either direction. As a result, it’s necessary to use the absolute value to remove the direction that the ball is using and just check for the speed at which it is moving.

💡 Encourage the ninja to test out the Ball sprite’s movement multiple times to make sure they have checked and set the sprite’s velocity correctly in the onHitWall event.
steps.instructions:
Now, the Ball sprite won’t stop bouncing! Add code to gradually reduce the Ball sprite’s bounce, so that the user is able to swing again.


Use an onHitWall event to control the speed of the Ball sprite’s bounce. Inside the event, check if the Ball sprite’s y-velocity is too large in either direction (bouncing up, or being pulled down). Open Math and drag [abs] inside the parentheses of the if condition. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: Math.abs(-1).


The abs function returns the absolute value of a number, or the value of a number without its sign (+/-). Update the parameter so that the condition checks if the absolute value of the Ball sprite’s y-velocity is greater than 50.


If so, use the throttle function to decrease the Ball sprite’s y-velocity by 50, every 500 ms. Else, set the Ball sprite’s y-velocity to 0.


Click ▶ to test what happens now when the Ball sprite hits any wall tile.

steps.hints:
❓ Did you declare a status bar sprite to be accessed throughout the project, like this?

let statusbar: StatusBarSprite = null
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What might the status bar indicate to the user? How does this improve the user experience of the project?

❓ Why is it useful to put all of the status bar’s code inside a function?

❓ Did you delete let in the statusbars.create function and update the sprite’s name, since the status bar sprite has already been declared?

 

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja to delete let and update the status bar sprite’s name (to the name used to declare the sprite under // project initialization) in the statusbars.create function inside the createStatusBar function.
steps.instructions:
Improve the user's experience by using a status bar to control the force that is used to hit the golf ball!


Add the status-bar extension to the project.


Under // project initialization, declare a status bar sprite by using the keyword let, the name of the sprite statusbar and a colon. Then, type StatusBarSprite, an assignment operator, and null. Because the sprite is declared outside of any block statements, it is a global variable and can be accessed throughout the project.


Define a createStatusBar function. Use the statusbars.create function to assign the status bar sprite width and height values. Set the status bar’s starting value to 0, and its max value to 100. Then, position it to appear in the top middle of the screen, relative to the camera’s position.


Use the setBarBorder function to update the width and color of the status bar’s outline. Set the fill and background color of the status bar. 


Then, call the createStatusBar function inside the conditional in the A button pressed event if the Ball sprite is not moving. Click ▶ to test the status bar’s appearance!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you nest a conditional to check if the value of the status bar is equal to 100 whenever the A button is repeated?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How does the countingUp variable control the status bar’s display?

❓ Why should the status bar’s value be updated inside on A button repeated event?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that Boolean variables are helpful for keeping track of game conditions in a project. In this example, the countingUp variable is keeping track of whether the status bar is visually increasing or decreasing in value. This is useful for triggering the status bar to reverse in direction, once a certain value is reached.

💡 The status bar’s value should be updated inside on A button repeated event so that the user can hold down the A button while the status bar’s value is updated, then the ball will be hit once the button is released.
steps.instructions:
Match the status bar’s value to the user’s actions!


Declare a countingUp variable set to false under // project initialization. This will be used to keep track of when the status bar’s value is increasing or decreasing.


Create an on A button repeated event under // project events. Inside the event, use a conditional to check if countingUp is true. 


Add code inside the conditional to move the Player sprite 0.2 pixels to the left, to visually show the force with which the club will hit the ball. Increase the status bar’s value by 2 to reflect the gradual change as the user presses and holds the A button.


Add a nested conditional that checks if the status bar has reached its maximum value, then change the value of the countingUp variable to false.


Click ▶ to see the status bar’s value and Player sprite’s position change as the user presses and holds the A button.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you change the Player sprite’s x-position by 0.2 and and the status bar’s value by -2, if countingUp is false ?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How does the countingUp variable control the status bar’s display?

❓ Why should the status bar’s value be updated inside on A button repeated event?

❓ Does the value of the status bar visually increase and decrease as expected, while the user presses and holds the A button?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that Boolean variables are helpful for keeping track of game conditions in a project. In this example, the countingUp variable is keeping track of whether the status bar is visually increasing or decreasing in value. This is useful for triggering the status bar to reverse in direction, once a certain value is reached.

💡 The status bar’s value should be updated inside on A button repeated event so that the user can hold down the A button while the status bar’s value is updated, then the ball will be hit once the button is released.

💡 Prompt the ninja to test the A button repeated event code. As they press and hold the A button, the status bar’s value should gradually increase and the Player sprite should move to the left. Once it reaches its maximum value, the status bar’s value should gradually decrease the Player sprite should back towards the right.
steps.instructions:
Decrease the value of the status bar once it reaches its maximum value!


Add an else if condition inside the on A button repeated event. Inside the parentheses, use a NOT operator to check if countingUp is false to see if the status bar’s value is decreasing.


Then, copy all of the code inside the if condition and paste it inside the curly brackets of the else if condition. 


Update the values in the code so that the Player sprite moves 0.2 pixels to the right and the status bar’s value decreases by 2. 


Inside the next conditional, check if the status bar has reached its minimum value, then change the value of the countingUp variable to true.


Click ▶ to test the status bar’s code, ensuring that it increases and decreases as the user presses the A button.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you update the value of force before the Ball sprite’s vx and vy values are set when the A button is released?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens to the value of the force variable when the A button is repeated and released?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the A button is repeated (or held down by the user), the status bar’s value gradually increases and decreases. During this process, when the A button is released by the user, the force variable’s value will be assigned the current status bar value, then multiplied by 2. As a result, the status bar determines the value of the force, which represents the amount of power and velocity that the golf ball will be hit with.
steps.instructions:
Set the Ball sprite’s force to the status bar’s value!


Under // project initialization, assign force a value of 0.


If the ball is not moving when the A button is released, destroy the status bar sprite so that it is no longer visible. Then, reassign force to the status bar’s value multiplied by 2.


Click ▶ to test how the status bar’s value changes the Ball sprite’s movement.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use the after function to make the Ball sprite invisible, showing it disappearing into the hole?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What sprite kind should be used in the onHitWall event?

❓ What happens when the user hits the ball into the hole?

❓ How does this improve the user experience?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja to change the sprite kind to Ball in the onHitWall event.

💡 When the Ball sprite overlaps the holeTile asset, the Ball sprite stops bouncing off walls and disappears after a short amount of time. This gives the appearance that the ball has fallen into the hole, simulating what would happen in real life.
steps.instructions:
Make something happen once the user hits the ball into the hole!


When the Ball sprite overlaps the holeTile asset, set the Ball sprite to stop bouncing on walls. After a short amount of time, set the Ball sprite’s Invisible flag on, so that it appears to fall into the hole.


Click ▶ to test out the completed first hole!

subgroups.introduction: Create the first hole of a mini golf project that uses physics and a status bar to control the movement of the golf ball.

validationItems.text: Display the levelOne tilemap and background image on screen.
Set the Ball sprite’s position, y-acceleration, x-friction, and for the camera to follow it. Set the Player sprite’s position relative to the Ball sprite.
Reset the Player sprite’s position when the A button is pressed.
Use variables to control the Ball sprite’s velocity. Code the Ball sprite to move when the A button is released, if it is not already moving.
Set the Ball sprite to bounce on walls when the A button is pressed and to gradually decrease its speed when it hits a wall.
Define a createStatusBar function to display a status bar on screen.
Change the value of the status bar when the A button is pressed and repeated.
Set the force variable to 0 at the beginning of the project, then reassign it to the status bar’s value multiplied by 2 and destroy the status bar when the A button is released.
Reset the Ball sprite when it overlaps the hole tile.
